title: Self-Adjoint and Normal Operators

We now study operators with special relationships to their adjoints. Throughout this section, $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner product space.

## <span class="num">9.4.1</span> Self-Adjoint Operators

The most important case is when $T = T^*$.

:::definition{9.4.1} Self-adjoint operator
An operator $T : V \to V$ is ***self-adjoint*** (or ***Hermitian***) if $T^* = T$, i.e., $$\langle v, T(w) \rangle = \langle T(v), w \rangle$$ for all $v, w \in V$.
:::

:::note
In an orthonormal basis, $T$ is self-adjoint iff its matrix is symmetric (real case, $M = M^t$) or Hermitian (complex case, $M = M^*$), by Theorem [9.3.4](/notes/math-55a/9-3-the-adjoint#theorem-9-3-4). Self-adjoint operators need not be invertible: for example, the zero operator is self-adjoint.
:::

:::proposition{9.4.2} Basic properties of self-adjoint operators
Let $T : V \to V$ be self-adjoint.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\langle T(v), v \rangle$ is real for all $v \in V$.
2. Every eigenvalue of $T$ is real.
3. Eigenvectors of $T$ for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
4. If $S \subseteq V$ is a $T$-invariant subspace, then $S^\perp$ is also $T$-invariant.
:::

:::proof
(i) $\langle T(v), v \rangle = \langle v, T(v) \rangle = \ol{\langle T(v), v \rangle}$.

(ii) If $T(v) = \lambda v$ with $v \neq 0$, then $\lambda \|v\|^2 = \langle v, T(v) \rangle = \langle T(v), v \rangle = \ol\lambda \|v\|^2$, so $\lambda = \ol\lambda$. (Over $\RR$ there is nothing to prove; the content is in the complex case.)

(iii) If $T(v) = \lambda v$ and $T(w) = \mu w$ with $\lambda \neq \mu$, then $\lambda$ is real by (ii), and $$\mu \langle v, w \rangle = \langle v, T(w) \rangle = \langle T(v), w \rangle = \ol{\lambda} \langle v, w \rangle = \lambda \langle v, w \rangle.$$ So $(\mu - \lambda)\langle v, w \rangle = 0$, and $\langle v, w \rangle = 0$.

(iv) This is Lemma [9.3.7](/notes/math-55a/9-3-the-adjoint#lemma-9-3-7)(i) with $T^* = T$.
:::

:::note
Property (iv) is what makes self-adjoint operators diagonalizable: once we find an eigenvector, its orthogonal complement is invariant, and we can proceed by induction.
:::

## <span class="num">9.4.2</span> The Spectral Theorem for Real Self-Adjoint Operators

Over $\CC$, every operator has an eigenvector. Over $\RR$, the main work is to show that a self-adjoint operator has one. The key is that quadratic polynomials without real roots cannot kill anything.

:::lemma{9.4.3} Positivity lemma
Let $T$ be self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional real inner product space. For any real $a > 0$, the operator $T^2 + a \cdot \id$ is invertible.
:::

:::proof
For $v \neq 0$, using $\langle T(T(v)), v \rangle = \langle T(v), T(v) \rangle$, $$\langle (T^2 + a \cdot \id)(v), v \rangle = \langle T^2(v), v \rangle + a \langle v, v \rangle = \|T(v)\|^2 + a \|v\|^2 > 0.$$ So $(T^2 + a \cdot \id)(v) \neq 0$ for $v \neq 0$. Thus $T^2 + a \cdot \id$ is injective, hence invertible since $V$ is finite-dimensional.
:::

:::corollary{9.4.4} Quadratics without real roots
If $p(x) = x^2 + bx + c \in \RR{}[x]$ has no real roots (i.e., $b^2 - 4c < 0$), and $T$ is self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional real inner product space, then $p(T) = T^2 + bT + c \cdot \id$ is invertible.
:::

:::proof
Complete the square: $T^2 + bT + c \cdot \id = (T + \frac{b}{2} \id)^2 + (c - \frac{b^2}{4}) \id$.

Since $b^2 - 4c < 0$, we have $a = c - \frac{b^2}{4} > 0$. The operator $S = T + \frac{b}{2} \id$ is self-adjoint ($S^* = T^* + \frac{b}{2} \id = S$ by Proposition [9.3.3](/notes/math-55a/9-3-the-adjoint#proposition-9-3-3)). By the lemma, $S^2 + a \cdot \id = p(T)$ is invertible.
:::

:::theorem{9.4.5} Spectral theorem (real self-adjoint operators)
Let $T : V \to V$ be a self-adjoint operator on a finite-dimensional real inner product space. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of $T$. In particular, $T$ is diagonalizable, and its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $\RR$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1: $T$ has an eigenvector if $V \neq 0$.** Let $n = \dim V \geq 1$ and choose any nonzero $v \in V$. The $n + 1$ vectors $v, T(v), \ldots, T^n(v)$ are linearly dependent, so there is a nonzero polynomial $p \in \RR{}[x]$ with $p(T)(v) = 0$. It is not constant, since a nonzero multiple of $v$ is nonzero.

Factor $p$ over $\RR$: $$p(x) = a \prod_i (x - \lambda_i) \prod_j (x^2 + b_j x + c_j),$$ with $a \neq 0$, $\lambda_i \in \RR$, and $b_j^2 - 4c_j < 0$. (Such a factorization exists by induction on $\deg p$. By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (Chapter 4), $p$ has a root $\mu \in \CC$. If $\mu$ is real, then $p = (x - \mu)q$ with $q \in \RR{}[x]$ by the factor theorem (Lemma [4.3.14](/notes/math-55a/4-3-polynomial-rings-and-field-extensions#lemma-4-3-14)). Otherwise $p(\ol\mu) = \ol{p(\mu)} = 0$ because $p$ has real coefficients, and since $\ol\mu \neq \mu$, applying the factor theorem twice in $\CC{}[x]$ gives $p = mq$ with $m = (x - \mu)(x - \ol\mu) = x^2 - 2\operatorname{Re}(\mu)\, x + |\mu|^2$, a real quadratic with no real roots. Conjugating all coefficients gives $p = m\ol q$, so $m(q - \ol q) = 0$, and $q = \ol q$ has real coefficients because $\CC{}[x]$ has no zero divisors (Lemma [4.3.3](/notes/math-55a/4-3-polynomial-rings-and-field-extensions#lemma-4-3-3)).) Since $q \mapsto q(T)$ is a ring homomorphism $\RR{}[x] \to \End(V)$, $$p(T) = a \prod_i (T - \lambda_i \id) \prod_j (T^2 + b_j T + c_j \id).$$ Each $T^2 + b_j T + c_j \id$ is invertible by the corollary. If every $T - \lambda_i \id$ were injective, then $p(T)$ would be a composite of injective operators, hence injective; but $p(T)(v) = 0$ with $v \neq 0$. So some $T - \lambda_i \id$ has a nonzero kernel, and $T$ has an eigenvector with real eigenvalue $\lambda_i$.

**Step 2: orthonormal eigenbasis, by induction on $\dim V$.** If $\dim V = 0$, the empty list works. Otherwise, by Step 1 let $v_1$ be an eigenvector with $T(v_1) = \lambda_1 v_1$, normalized so $\|v_1\| = 1$. Let $S = \operatorname{span}(v_1)$. Since $T(S) \subseteq S$, the orthogonal complement $S^\perp$ is $T$-invariant (Proposition [9.4.2](/notes/math-55a/9-4-self-adjoint-and-normal-operators#proposition-9-4-2)(iv)), and $\dim S^\perp = \dim V - 1$.

Since $S^\perp$ is invariant under $T = T^*$, the restriction $T|_{S^\perp}$ is self-adjoint for the restricted inner product (Lemma [9.3.7](/notes/math-55a/9-3-the-adjoint#lemma-9-3-7)(ii)). By induction, $S^\perp$ has an orthonormal basis $\{v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ of eigenvectors of $T$. Then $(v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n)$ is an orthonormal list of length $n$, hence an orthonormal basis of $V$, consisting of eigenvectors.

**Step 3: the characteristic polynomial.** In this basis $T$ has the diagonal matrix $\diag(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$ with $\lambda_i \in \RR$, so its characteristic polynomial is $\prod_i (x - \lambda_i)$ (Definition [7.4.7](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#definition-7-4-7)).
:::

:::note
The spectral theorem says that self-adjoint operators on real inner product spaces are “as nice as possible”: they are diagonalizable, with real eigenvalues, and the eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal (Proposition [9.4.2](/notes/math-55a/9-4-self-adjoint-and-normal-operators#proposition-9-4-2)(iii)). The matrix in an orthonormal eigenbasis is $\diag(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$. In matrix terms: for every real symmetric matrix $A$ there is a matrix $P$ with $P^t P = I$ (its columns are the orthonormal eigenvectors) such that $P^{-1} A P = P^t A P$ is diagonal.
:::

### Skew-Adjoint Operators

The “opposite” of self-adjoint is skew-adjoint.

:::definition{9.4.6} Skew-adjoint operator
An operator $T : V \to V$ is ***skew-adjoint*** (or ***anti-self-adjoint***) if $T^* = -T$, i.e., $$\langle v, T(w) \rangle = -\langle T(v), w \rangle$$ for all $v, w \in V$.
:::

:::note
In an orthonormal basis, $T$ is skew-adjoint iff its matrix $M$ satisfies $M^t = -M$ (real case) or $M^* = -M$ (complex case). Such matrices are called ***skew-symmetric*** and ***skew-Hermitian***, respectively.
:::

:::proposition{9.4.7} Properties of skew-adjoint operators
Let $T : V \to V$ be skew-adjoint on a finite-dimensional real inner product space.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\langle T(v), v \rangle = 0$ for all $v \in V$.
2. The only possible eigenvalue of $T$ is $0$.
3. $\id + T$ is invertible.
:::

:::proof
(i) Taking $w = v$ in the definition gives $\langle v, T(v) \rangle = -\langle T(v), v \rangle$. Over $\RR$, $\langle v, T(v) \rangle = \langle T(v), v \rangle$, so $2\langle T(v), v \rangle = 0$.

(ii) If $T(v) = \lambda v$ with $v \neq 0$, then $\lambda \|v\|^2 = \langle T(v), v \rangle = 0$ by (i), so $\lambda = 0$.

(iii) If $(\id + T)(v) = 0$, then $T(v) = -v$; by (ii), $-1$ is not an eigenvalue, so $v = 0$. Thus $\id + T$ is injective, hence invertible since $V$ is finite-dimensional.
:::

:::note
Over $\RR$, a skew-adjoint operator can have no eigenvalues at all: rotation by $\pi/2$ in $\RR^2$, with matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$, is skew-adjoint. Its eigenvalues as a complex matrix are $\pm i$; Corollary [9.4](/notes/math-55a/9-4-self-adjoint-and-normal-operators) below shows that the complex eigenvalues of a real skew-symmetric matrix are always purely imaginary.
:::

## <span class="num">9.4.3</span> Normal Operators and the Complex Spectral Theorem

Over $\CC$, the spectral theorem extends to a larger class of operators: those that commute with their adjoint.

:::definition{9.4.8} Normal operator
An operator $T : V \to V$ is ***normal*** if $$T T^* = T^* T.$$
:::

:::example{9.4.9} Classes of normal operators
- Self-adjoint operators ($T^* = T$) are normal: $TT^* = T^2 = T^*T$.
- Skew-adjoint operators ($T^* = -T$) are normal: $TT^* = -T^2 = T^*T$.
- Operators with $T^* = T^{-1}$ are normal: $TT^* = \id = T^*T$. These are the orthogonal and unitary operators of Section [9.5](/notes/math-55a/9-5-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators).
:::

:::lemma{9.4.10} Characterization of normality
An operator $T$ is normal if and only if $\|T(v)\| = \|T^*(v)\|$ for all $v \in V$.
:::

:::proof
By the defining property of the adjoint and $(T^*)^* = T$, $$\begin{aligned}
\|T(v)\|^2 &= \langle T(v), T(v) \rangle = \langle T^*T(v), v \rangle, \\
\|T^*(v)\|^2 &= \langle T^*(v), T^*(v) \rangle = \langle TT^*(v), v \rangle.
\end{aligned}$$ So $\|T(v)\| = \|T^*(v)\|$ for all $v$ iff $\langle S(v), v \rangle = 0$ for all $v$, where $S = T^*T - TT^*$. If $T$ is normal, $S = 0$. Conversely, $S$ is self-adjoint (Proposition [9.3.3](/notes/math-55a/9-3-the-adjoint#proposition-9-3-3)), and we claim that a self-adjoint $S$ with $\langle S(v), v \rangle = 0$ for all $v$ is zero. For any $v, w$, $$\begin{aligned}
0 &= \langle S(v + w), v + w \rangle - \langle S(v), v \rangle - \langle S(w), w \rangle \\
&= \langle S(v), w \rangle + \langle S(w), v \rangle = \langle S(v), w \rangle + \ol{\langle S(v), w \rangle},
\end{aligned}$$ using $\langle S(w), v \rangle = \langle w, S(v) \rangle = \ol{\langle S(v), w \rangle}$. So $\operatorname{Re}\langle S(v), w \rangle = 0$. Over $\RR$ this says $\langle S(v), w \rangle = 0$. Over $\CC$, replacing $w$ by $iw$ gives $0 = \operatorname{Re}(i\langle S(v), w \rangle) = -\operatorname{Im}\langle S(v), w \rangle$. In both cases $\langle S(v), w \rangle = 0$ for all $w$; taking $w = S(v)$ gives $S(v) = 0$.
:::

:::proposition{9.4.11} Normal operators and eigenspaces
Let $T$ be normal.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. If $T(v) = \lambda v$, then $T^*(v) = \ol{\lambda} v$.
2. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
3. $\ker(T - \lambda \id) = \ker(T^* - \ol{\lambda} \id)$.
:::

:::proof
(i) The operator $T - \lambda \id$ is normal: its adjoint is $T^* - \ol{\lambda} \id$, and these two commute since $T$ and $T^*$ commute. By the lemma, $\|T^*(v) - \ol{\lambda} v\| = \|T(v) - \lambda v\| = 0$, so $T^*(v) = \ol{\lambda} v$.

(ii) If $T(v) = \lambda v$ and $T(w) = \mu w$ with $\lambda \neq \mu$, then by (i) $$\mu \langle v, w \rangle = \langle v, T(w) \rangle = \langle T^*(v), w \rangle = \langle \ol{\lambda} v, w \rangle = \lambda \langle v, w \rangle.$$ So $(\mu - \lambda)\langle v, w \rangle = 0$, giving $v \perp w$.

(iii) The inclusion $\subseteq$ is (i). Since $T^*$ is also normal, with $(T^*)^* = T$, applying (i) to $T^*$ and the eigenvalue $\ol\lambda$ gives the reverse inclusion.
:::

:::theorem{9.4.12} Complex spectral theorem
Let $T : V \to V$ be a normal operator on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of $T$. Moreover:

- if $T$ is self-adjoint, its eigenvalues are real;
- if $T$ is skew-adjoint, its eigenvalues are purely imaginary;
- if $T^* = T^{-1}$ (i.e., $T$ is unitary, Section [9.5](/notes/math-55a/9-5-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators)), its eigenvalues lie on the unit circle $|\lambda| = 1$.
:::

:::proof
We induct on $n = \dim V$; the case $n = 0$ is trivial. Let $n \geq 1$. Since $\CC$ is algebraically closed, $T$ has an eigenvector (Theorem [7.5.1](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-1)); let $v_1$ be a unit eigenvector with $T(v_1) = \lambda v_1$.

By Proposition [9.4.11](/notes/math-55a/9-4-self-adjoint-and-normal-operators#proposition-9-4-11)(i), $T^*(v_1) = \ol{\lambda} v_1$. So $S = \operatorname{span}(v_1)$ is invariant under both $T$ and $T^*$. By Lemma [9.3.7](/notes/math-55a/9-3-the-adjoint#lemma-9-3-7)(i), applied to $T$ and to $T^*$ (using $(T^*)^* = T$), the subspace $W = S^\perp$ is invariant under both $T^*$ and $T$. By Lemma [9.3.7](/notes/math-55a/9-3-the-adjoint#lemma-9-3-7)(ii), $(T|_W)^* = T^*|_W$, so $$T|_W (T|_W)^* = (TT^*)|_W = (T^*T)|_W = (T|_W)^* T|_W,$$ and $T|_W$ is normal. Since $\dim W = n - 1$, by induction $W$ has an orthonormal basis $\{v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ of eigenvectors of $T$. Then $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis of $V$.

For the eigenvalues: if $T(v) = \lambda v$ with $v \neq 0$, then $T^*(v) = \ol\lambda v$. If $T^* = T$, this gives $\ol\lambda = \lambda$. If $T^* = -T$, it gives $\ol\lambda = -\lambda$. If $T^* = T^{-1}$, then $v = T^*(T(v)) = \ol\lambda \lambda v$, so $|\lambda|^2 = 1$.
:::

:::note
The complex spectral theorem is stronger than the real one: every normal operator (not just every self-adjoint one) is diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis. The price is working over $\CC$ with Hermitian inner products. Normality is also necessary: if $T$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis, its matrix $D$ in that basis is diagonal, $T^*$ has the diagonal matrix $D^* = \ol D$, and diagonal matrices commute, so $T$ is normal.
:::

:::corollary{9.4.13} Eigenvalues of real symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix, and consider its complex eigenvalues (the roots in $\CC$ of its characteristic polynomial).

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. If $A^t = A$, all complex eigenvalues of $A$ are real.
2. If $A^t = -A$, all complex eigenvalues of $A$ are purely imaginary.
3. If $A^t A = I$, all complex eigenvalues of $A$ have absolute value $1$.
:::

:::proof
Let $T : \CC^n \to \CC^n$, $T(z) = Az$, with the standard Hermitian inner product. The standard basis is orthonormal, so $T^*$ has matrix $A^* = A^t$ (the entries of $A$ are real). Thus $T$ is self-adjoint in case (i), skew-adjoint in case (ii), and satisfies $T^* = T^{-1}$ in case (iii). The roots of the characteristic polynomial of $A$ are the eigenvalues of $T$, and the theorem applies.
:::
